projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dorinda Guillermo was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: I'm Dorinda Guillermo. I should say, I'm Dorinda Guillermo, formerly from the Philippines, born and raised in the Philippines and educated the early years of my college life. And I came to the United States in 1961 and -- and I'm a naturalized American citizen. So... well, is that all?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: If we can get your address and the city -- we have that. Your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: My date of birth is January 23rd, 1927.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Your place of birth was the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Manila, Philippines.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Your branch of service or wartime activity?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: My wartime activities, I was with the intelligence unit part -- part time, and then later on I moved to another unit, a guerilla unit. This was right after the Philippines was occupied by the Japanese, so the guerilla units were formed all over the country to fight the Japanese after the fall of Bataan and Corregidor.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: So you weren't actually -- you were in a resistance --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. I was in the --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- movement?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: I was in the -- yeah, I was in the resistance movement.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: So were there any ranks or anything?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, according to my -- according to my records, I was a -- I was -- I was a staff sergeant.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: A staff sergeant.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Did they give you any sort of serial number or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No, they didn't give me, but I -- what I understand is we were under -- we were classified under TDG, terminal date guerillas. Yeah, TDG, yeah. We didn't have -- I didn't have a serial number.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: What were the dates that you were involved in this?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Okay. Let's see. Okay. This is... let me see. October 15th, 1943, up to... let's see. The time I was honorably discharged from the military service of the Philippine Commonwealth, the mobilization authority general order number, up to February 9th -- February -- 19th February `46.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: And what age were you then?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: I beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Your age at that time?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, I was 16 and a half when I was inducted, so...

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: So this is during the Second World War then, --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- right? During the Japanese occupation.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. During the Japanese occupation, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Did you sustain any wartime injuries?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: No injuries?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Maybe malaria.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: I think that should count.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: But I -- but I -- but I got over it, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No. I wish they sent me a list of men, non-com.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: We should state on the recording that we are at Dorinda Guillermo's house at 130 West Oak Street in West Lafayette --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: East. East Oak.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Oh, pardon me.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. No wonder. You went to West Oak --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: No, no, no. We did East Oak. I apologize. I live over on West Oak.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Anyway, what was the first thing -- my name is Dorinda, D-o-r-i-n-d-a.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Dorinda.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh, D-o-r-i-n-d-a.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Pardon me.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Does that name not appear on my records?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: And my name is Bob Thrash, and this is Sung Hee --

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Park.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Sung Hee Park.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- Park, who are doing the interview for EDCI 615, Educational Curriculum Design at Purdue University. And I guess we can kinda start. Is that --

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Yeah. We need to record today's date.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Ah.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: June 24th.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: What caused you to get involved in this? Were you drafted into the service or did you volunteer?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No. The thing that happened was -- the thing that happened was the intelligence unit where my uncle was an officer by then -- his name was Major Liberty and he was with the intelligence.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: In the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: In the Philippines. They started -- they started meeting in my -- in our house, and that got me into it. And when they met, I had to be such like a watch dog, you know, because Japanese soldiers were -- would be passing by off and on our place while the meeting was going on inside the house.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Was -- was your father then with -- with the Philippine Army?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No, my father was not with the Philippine Army, but he was involved also in that other intelligence unit. Because my father was -- he was the chief of the employment section of the Manila City Hall, the city government, and the Japanese Navy officers used to come and ask for laborers to work in their Navy yards and all that. So one day my father -- one day my father was -- was invited by one of the Naval officers to their headquarters in one of the former government -- Philippine government buildings where the Navy -- Japanese Navy was housed, and they didn't know my father was an intelligence officer. And he looked around, he looked around, see what he could find. And so after that -- well, he -- the thing was, he was escorted other places since he was being shown what they had and why they needed these people, you know. And one of the thing -- one of the things that the employment division had to do was to supply laborers to companies and -- and whatever agencies asked for. And so my father would look for that because it was an employment agency office. So anyway, after that my father went back to his office and started writing his report on what he saw. And -- and right after -- oh. While he -- he told me this story, because he said to me, "I thought I'll never see you again." The thing was, he went back to his office and started typing what he saw as his -- as his report. And then what happened was this Naval officer was rather nervous, became panicky, you know, and he didn't even stop by the receptionist's table. You know, he just went inside my father's office. And so my father also at that time was thrown out, you know, felt that feeling of being thrown -- you know, being in some situation. But obviously the Japanese officer didn't -- didn't read English, and so he was saved from that. And then later on when he came home he said, "I -- I -- I thought I will never see you again," he told me, and he told me this story. And I didn't know that he was writing -- that he was in this intelligence group at one point. And so this group, the Hunter's (ph) ROTC guerillas, this was the guerilla unit that I was involved with in the city of Manila, they kept coming into our house, and they met there for strategic planning and all those things. And we did have several people there that I could remember. Of course, my uncle was Major Liberty. Some of them were not using their names. One was a buxom woman who was named Madam -- Madam X, and she always wear -- always wore a black dress. And then also we had a Mrs. El- -- Mrs. Elsworth. I think her husband was with the U.S. Armed Forces. And she had the baby girl in a pack that she used to take around with her during the meetings. And then there were -- the Hunter's ROTC guerillas, a good number of them were former students of the Philippine Military Academy. And then some also -- a good number of them also were formerly ROTC cadets and ROTC officers in the universities and colleges in Manila, because at that time our ROTC program was very active prior to --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: The what program? I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: ROTC.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: ROTC?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, was very active in the Philippines because that was one of their recog- -- I think that was what -- one of the things that was introduced into the Philippines, I think, by General MacArthur. When he became the military advisor to the Philippine Commonwealth government and the Philippine Commonwealth president, that was one of the things that he requested or maybe asked, that 20 years old will be drafted into the military Army, Philippine Army. And so -- and so the ROTC was a very strong program in the Philippines at that time, and most of the officers of these Hunter's ROTC guerillas -- that's one reason they have the ROTC guerillas -- were former officer -- students of the Philippine Military Academy and also our ROTC officers schooled at colleges in the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: How did you become involved? Did they meet for a while in your house?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: And then how -- how did -- I mean, you were so young.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, I was so young. I was a -- sort of a watch dog. They asked me to look around and see, you know, when the Japanese would start coming in, you know, around the -- by -- on the street and all those things, you know. Because the Japanese military -- Japanese soldiers were always on the go, looking for people or whatever. And the thing that happened was... I could remember the time when -- I could remember the time when we had all those -- across the house was the gymnasium of one of the -- gymnasium of the University of Santa Tomas in the Philippines. It was across our street, because our house was just across the university campus. And that campus at that time, the whole -- the whole campus was used as an interment camp for American citizens and allied citizens, like Mexicans and English. They were all interred there. And I could remember the time that... 16 years old, you know. Maybe I wasn't as fearful or whatever. But I could remember, we could go to the second -- second story of the house. And, of course, the window of the gymnasium also opened. The window by our house also were so adjacent to each other that once in a while we -- we would raise the Philippine -- the American flag. We used to have American flag because we were under the United States at that time. And then -- or else we would -- there were two children with me, too, and we would write messages, you know, big enough, that said, "God bless America" and something like that. And then we would make the V sign, you know. But we were in the inner part of the room, you know, not by the -- not exactly by the window because we know we will be seen there. So we tried to give encouragement to those -- to those interment -- internees. They were called internees. And I got involved because at that time they told me to be -- kept -- to be kept -- to be a watch dog for them, see where -- how and when the Japanese are coming. And if they are coming, I'll get to tell them so that they could disperse. But there were no untoward incidents at that time. So anyway, eventually our house became a store house, a store house where some of the Filipinos who were in sympathy with the guerilla forces would make hand-rolled cigarettes. And then some of them would also bring -- would also donate foodstuffs, like dried fish, small fish, dried fish, you know, and also fish sauce that they could use in the -- in the mountains, because most of the guerillas were -- were using the mountains as their -- as their habitat. And -- and some of them were -- started to compose songs. Like, if I could translate it from our Filipino language to American -- to English, it -- some of the songs would say, "If in case I do not come back, you will find my body in the mountains." And then some -- one -- one song also states like this, "the life of a guerilla is so harsh, always in danger, and our life is always at stake." That is -- and I have learned that and -- I have learned that song, but I couldn't remember the last verses. I can see the three -- three -- three sentences, you know, and then I stop. I wonder, what are the rest, you know? So I have learned those. And then when the couriers from the mountains would come, then they pick up those supplies and then brought them back to the mountains. That was the -- the most part that I did.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: How did you feel? Were you scared or was -- must have been --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: I don't know. Maybe because as a 16-year-old, you know, you think you're just so carefree and everything.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Even in the first days, --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- when you first started doing this?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Do you remember the first time that you had to go watch or --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No, I can't remember it. But I just peek, maybe, out first at the -- peek, peek. I'll go out a little bit by the door, you know, and then look or something. But I never was scared. And then also -- plus, the people in the house were very -- they were very friendly, and I didn't -- I wasn't scared of them.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Did you have any training that you were involved with or did they train you --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- to do any of these things?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No. They didn't train me anything. They didn't do -- I just maybe learned on the job or whatever to do, you know.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: On-the-job training.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: On-the-job training. But anyway, one of -- well, in 1944 the situation was getting harder and food was getting scarce. And because of my father's experiences in the -- with me, the daughter he had, he stopped. My -- I was in a dangerous position because the Japanese would -- if they then _________ or whatever, if they -- even in their good minds, they would rape you or take you and, you know, some -- done something like that without any reason at all. And so I could remember -- I could remember my father telling me, he said, "This place is not a good place for you. I think we will have to go to the province," he said. Because earlier that year all of my siblings went to my home -- my father's hometown in the province of Cayagan by the coastal town of Appari, and we were -- my uncle became a prosperous lumberman, and he had all the money to -- to spend for -- to take my siblings back with him to the province and to feed them and to -- you know, to support them. So my father said, "Okay," he said, "you can take them." But I -- I -- I decided to stay with my father because I said I -- he needed somebody to take care of his -- to take care of him. And so my father said, "Oh, that's a good idea." That's what he said, so...

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: The province was not under control of the Japanese government?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Which one?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Where you -- where you would have went that was safe, that was a safe place.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: At that time it was a better place than Manila. Because in Manila you did not know who were -- who were the true Filipinos and who were not. You would be mixing with Filipinos there, all of a sudden the Japanese will come up on you, and find out that they're among the people you have been -- as you're shaking or talking, they are the Japanese. So it was a dangerous place. So my father said, "Well, this is getting to be a dangerous place, plus the food's getting scarce, so I better take you to the province." So we boarded a Japanese ship and we sailed for four or five days going to the -- going home to my father's hometown. And while he was there, at one point he decided to go back to Manila because we needed medical supplies. And when he was in Manila, the Hunter's ROTC guerillas raided the national penitentiary and tried to free some of those prisoners, war prisoners there, and my father knew what has happened. And so he went back -- after taking all the medical supplies, he went back to the province with us. And then in September of 1944 my father and I were out in the inner -- in another town called Allacapan, and we were supposed to have a big party on September 11th and -- because at that time those -- those -- the province -- that province, Cayagan province, was -- food was abundant. Rice, everything, was abundant. In fact, people from other sections of the country were coming in to barter for food. And so we went to that other town to get the food supplies for the party. And the day before, I left my father in -- in my uncle's house, thinking -- because he told me that, "You better go ahead. Anyway, you are going home tomorrow. We will bring all the supplies besides what you are bringing today." So we went to the riverbank. But on the way back -- on the way to the riverbank, I remembered I didn't kiss my father good-bye. Because that has always been a practice in our family. When you leave the house, you kiss your father good-bye. When you enter the house, you kiss your parents good-bye -- or greeting them, you know, with a kiss or something. So I was in the middle of the trail and I said, "I think I need to go back." But I was scared because I didn't know whether I'll be lost in the trail because that place was unfamiliar to me. So I just said to myself, well, anyway, he's coming back tomorrow so I can see him tomorrow, you know. The next day, my father and the rest of our menfolks were caught, were arrested by the Japanese, and this was the work of a Filipino spy. My father had always been a labor man. Prior to the war he was the senior assistant inspector of labor in the Department of Labor in the Philippines and he always worked in the Labor Department ever since. So this Filipino spy, this unfortunately was an Army officer, Filipino Army officer. He unfortunately came into the house barging and he said, "The Japanese military police are at my" -- no, "The Japanese are at my back," he said. And when he said that, he said -- he asked if there were so -- there were many -- if there were guns around, you know. So, well, my father said that there's nothing in there. He said no. And anyway, the Japanese people came, you know. They was posing as Japanese employers, and they told my father -- {telephone ringing.} It is okay. We'll just let that ring. Well, they told me father that they were establishing a lumber company in Appari, you know, in the town where we -- where we were there, and said that we were establishing a lumber company, and then, "we are -- we are looking for people to work with us." And so all of our menfolks gathered around. And so my father started asking questions to his brother, "Would you like to be a part of the -- of the force?" "Sure," said my uncle. So they -- so his name was written down. Then he called another uncle and he said, "Yes," you know. Then another cousin. "No," said that other cousin, then another one. I think there must have been about six of them or seven who were asked if they would want. And finally, what happened was, they had a list of people -- the Japanese had the list of people that they wanted and the names of the people that were listed there by my father ________ the names that they had. And finally they were arrested and taken to the Japanese military police headquarters in Appari. And they were interrogated and they were also tortured. Like my uncle, when they were trying to get answers from him, he didn't like to divulge anything, so they put a -- a wooden plank across him. They -- at first they make him drink a lot of water, and then two military police stood at each end and tried to seesaw him, made a seesaw out of him. And then when my father's time came for interrogation, the Japanese military police asked him, "are you an officer?" My father didn't answer. And then he said, "Brigadier General?" "Yes." Although he found out that if you are an officer, you're not be -- you will not be punished or tortured, you know. Because the first ones were -- were tortured, you know, after the interrogation. But my -- I felt that my father said, well, he did say that he was a brigadier general. It was the Japanese who ask him, and he said, "Well, yes, I am," you know. So that was what -- you see, my father sometimes has this -- I think he has -- he knows. He was a lawyer by profession, and so you can -- so he knows how to answer. So anyway, they stayed there for about three weeks. And in the meantime -- in the meantime, we brought their food and clothes. And one of the things that really meant so much to me was the two times I tried to see him. We were not allowed to visit. The only thing that they asks us was -- the only thing that we can do at that time is to bring their food in, and clothes, and then a Japanese officer would take them upstairs to where they were held. And one Sunday morning I was -- I was asked to take food to them. And at that time, when I finished bringing the food or giving the food to the Japanese officer, I saw my father by the porch. There was a porch, you know, on the second floor. And I was on the ground, and I looked at him. Then he turned his back against me. By the time he look -- he turned around again to see me, I saw him crying. And that really was one of the saddest moments of my life. And I just felt like flying home and saying -- I ran and ran, you know, and said, "I saw him, I saw him, I saw him." And I cried and I cried and I cried. And so they asked me, "Well, what did you see," like my sisters and my aunts, you know. And at that time, while they were there, we were also harassed by the Japanese military police.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Harassed?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Harassed, yeah. And one -- one afternoon my aunt, who was -- whose husband was Major Liberty, you know, my uncle who was with the intelligence, whenever the Japanese would come, he would start having convulsions because he had heart -- a heart condition. And they were looking for the picture of my uncle, and so they asked us if there were pictures. Sure, we have -- I could remember that time because I was scared. That was the time that I really was scared, that I could see my -- you know, my chin would be doing chattering, my teeth would be chattering. So I really didn't know what to feel about that. So -- but anyway, the thing was, they were looking for the picture of Major Liberty. And so we brought out all the pictures. And then incidentally there was a picture of my father with two of his co-lawyers, you know, but my father's picture was cut off. And so they became suspicious and they said, "Where is this part," you know? Incidentally, we had a copy of that picture to. And so we said "Here." And then at that time, when my father was -- and all the menfolks that we had were arrested, there were only two friends who came around the house. We seemed to be ostracized by the whole -- by the whole town. But there were two friends who came and asked us where we were -- how we were.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Do you think that the people there were afraid that if --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- they associated with you --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- they would also be harassed?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh. And then in the middle of the night they would come. You could hear the boots tramping, you know.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: The Japanese?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, the Japanese boots. And then we would go on the steps. In the middle of the night, twelve o'clock at night, while you are asleep. And then all of a sudden -- and then you have two lights -- because at that time there were no electricity. You know, we had to light candles or lamps, you know. And they were still harassing us, questioning about Major Liberty and also about the incident that my father had, you know, when he went back to Manila for medical supplies, if we knew anything about the raid down by the Hunter's ROTC guerillas. Well, how do we know? You know, my father never said anything about it. And later on, in fact, because we -- they couldn't get anything from us, they would throw their revolvers in front of us, just in front of us this way.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: To scare you?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, to scare us. So -- so anyway, in the last part of September they were brought to Manila.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Your father.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, my father. In fact, we came to know it because some of the townspeople saw them, their hands tied, and they were in a Japanese Army truck and they were in a corner of the street in town. And somebody came to our house and they said, "You better come and see what is happening to your father," he said, "because they're out there. They might be taking them away." So my aunt and I, my uncle's wife, you know, my brother -- my father's brother, she and I ran and ran to the place where the truck was located, but the truck was gone. And so we ran and ran. They sent us across town to the -- across the bridge, you know. Found out there was nothing, so we came back. So very discouraged and -- because we really didn't know that -- if anything, something will happen that they'll never come back again. So in the midst of that, in September -- in October we had the first air raid. The United States Air Force came raiding the town of Appari. And so we had to go to -- we had to use air raid shelters. We had air raid shelters in the Methodist Church which was at the back of our house.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Were you warned so that the innocent people would not be hurt or...

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, we were warned to build air raid shelters prior to that. And so we start -- we started having air raid shelters. And then on that October day -- I couldn't remember the day, but that is October 1944 the first air raid came. And the following day we decided to evacuate the town, to leave the town. And so we left and went back -- and went to Allacapan, you know, the first -- the second town from Appari, Allacapan, where my father was caught. We went back there because it's full of forests, it's full of timber. And incidentally, in that town there was another guerilla force that was working there, and I got involved in that, too, and I became the first-aider.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: A first-aider?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: A first-aider. I was with the medical --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Medical?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: -- medical corps. And so I worked there. And for a while I was with that group. And I could also remember the time when we went to -- we were close to the firing line in another town. This is -- this is something of an experience I've never had in my life because I've never ridden a caribou. Because at that time, you see, you have to either walk -- the guerilla --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: You had never ridden in a car at that point?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: The car?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Is that what you said? I misunderstood.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No. Okay. I have never ridden, shall I say, in caribou, the water buffalo.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Those -- that is the -- the water buffalo horns is -- oh, let me just show you. Tape paused.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: ...with him through this other town because we were supposed to be -- we were supposed to be helping medically. And at that time it was already close to -- it was 1945 when the United States Forces started -- well, they came back in October `44, but they started fighting, you know, with the Japanese. And there was this fighting being done by the Philippine Army forces under this guerilla unit.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: How close -- were you actually in the combat, involved with the combat?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: I couldn't remember how many -- not exactly miles, I don't think, because we can hear everything, all the -- all the exchange of guns and everything. And fortunately we were told to go back, to leave -- to leave that place and go back. So we went to Ballesteros. We went to Ballesteros, and at that time we were ready to go back to Appari. And Appari was razed to the ground at that time. And then at that point the U.S. military started to help the civilians coming back. And so they organized what they called the Philippine Civilians Affairs Unit and then they started helping people to -- not exactly resettle, but help with whatever they can, because the place was so razed to the ground. Nothing stood. Even the church where we had been very sheltered was really razed to the ground. And so it started people rebuilding. And we worked -- I worked in the PICAU hospital from there. And -- and then later on, I think it must be in `45, we were called to Manila to be interviewed because they asked that -- they asked that -- they asked for our names in the organized roster. And so you can see here -- you can see here, it says, to whom -- this is to certify that the name of Omaya (ph) Dorinda is carried as staff sergeant in the guerilla constructed roster of the headquarters company, second battalion MVR. That's mike veer (ph) battalion. It says Hunter's ROTC. In date of recognition of unit years 1945, January `45, limiting date of recognition, non-revised date of recognition, 7 May `42 in Folder 85, Page 45. So that's -- those are my records. And then this one says here, it says how much I was paid. It says here, records in this office show that one staff sergeant Omaya Dorinda, formerly with the headquarters company second -- second battalion mike veer (ph) regiment, Hunter's ROTC, a member of the Army of the Philippines in the service of the United States Armed Forces was paid arrears in pay computed, pay back monthly, base pay and quarters -- quarter allowance, highest rank, in the amount of 88 pesos -- 888 pesos and 36 cents -- 38 cents. The rate of exchange at that time was one is to two, one dollar to two pesos, so divided by two. So that means only how many? Forty-four -- let me see. Yeah, divided by two.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Close to 400 --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Close to -- 44-something, 44-something. So anyway --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: A month?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. No. That is the whole --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: The whole --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: The whole --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: The whole amount?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: The whole service.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: The whole time you serve, yeah. And then it says here, apparent pay of a staff sergeant is 60 pesos -- that is 30 dollars -- as of January 1945. That is one reason why we are asking for the equity -- equity law. That's why -- a reason why we are working on the -- to pass the bill, HR 491, which has something to do with the equity -- equity law recognizing the Philippine veterans' work during World War II, so that they can be compensated in line with the -- in line with the U.S. Armed Forces. And I had an article which appeared in the Journal Courier about that. And, well, the latest news that I have received from -- from the Philippine news is, I think they have considered -- our president has considered putting it in the budget, a certain amount of -- I don't know how many million dollars to --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Compensate?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: -- to compensate. So I don't know if that budget will be approved or not. So that is what I have done during...

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: If you don't mind, if it's not too painful, what eventually happened to your father?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: My father was killed by the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: He was?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: And then --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: While he was in prison?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. They were -- the -- the story's like this: People who survived -- there were ten of them who were taken. Some of them were friends, some of them were relatives. And a few relatives came back because they were freed, you know, when the Armed Forces came. And my -- one of my cousins died, because they were -- as prisoners, they were only fed with rice -- a handful of rice, and then you know the sweet potato leaves? We eat -- we eat sweet potato leaves in the Philippines. And then they just boiled that and used it as soup and then put it in the rice. That was what they subsisted on so -- as prisoners of war. And then what happened was, this cousin of mine, when he was freed by the liberation forces, he saw all this kind of food that was served to him, and he -- and he already -- they were given portions only because they knew that their stomach were not strong, you know. They were given that portion. And after he -- he had eaten his portion, he saw the other fellow prisoner, his portion was not finished, and he said, "Can I have that?" And so he ate it. And he died from that because his stomach couldn't -- you know, I mean, maybe his digestive system was not strong enough.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: But anyway, those who survived said that they used to play judo. You know, they used to have judo, jujitsu.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Martial arts, yeah.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh. And when it turned on my father's, he would say -- because he was the oldest in the group, and he would tell the boys that "Slowly, slowly," he said. He didn't want to be thrown, you know, and break his bones or something like that. And then one day, out of the ten of them, a Japanese military police said "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Tomorrow, off," like this, which means they will cut neck. And then "One, two, three, four, five," he said, "here," which means they will not be killed, you know. So they were killed -- they were brought to the old Chinese cemetery in Manila and they were cut necked. And they were buried in one common grave that later on, the liberation forces, when they came, they exhumed all the -- they exhumed all the bodies and placed them in boxes, and then they buried them in what they used to call the U.S. Military Cemetery Number 2 in Manila. And we also heard this from -- we heard this from the stilmonese (ph) of the Japanese military police when they record -- when they were brought before the War Crimes Commission. And my sister attended the War Crimes Commission trial of these Japanese military officers from our town and they -- this is what they told us. That's how we knew that they were -- that they were killed. And my -- my -- you know, it's so... you know, I think when the Japanese -- we saw the Japanese Army being captured by the liberation forces when we got into our town, and they were treated so well by the Japanese military police -- by the -- by the U.S. military police. Not even one of us could throw a stone at them. Not even one of us could do any harm on them 'cause they were prisoners of war and we were what you call -- we were complying with what they call the Geneva --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Convention?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: -- Convention, you know. And so when my sister attended the War Crimes Commission, the only thing that she could do was to stuck -- stuck her tongue -- to do was to stick her tongue out to those Japanese military police. So that -- so we really did quite -- we really had a lot of... and then they also tried to burn our house when they were looking for my uncle, Major Liberty. But it was good, some neighbors found -- saw the torch that they threw inside the house.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: As you reflect back now, years later, what do you think would motivate the Japanese --
[End of Tape]

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, I think -- I knew what -- some of the Koreans -- some of the Armed Forces were Korean people, Korean men.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: For the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Because they -- they at first to bring the Korean people to the Army. Actually, they don't want, but kind of for enforcement. So to save their life, they just get into the Army.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. They had some of -- because Korea was under Japan, too, so they took them. And you know what? They said that the fall of Bataan and Corregidor was something that -- that tried to save democracy in the Pacific. Because if they didn't, if the -- if the Philippine Armed Forces and also the Bataan forces did not maintain what they needed to do, they could have started what they call the Japanese -- they started this campaign called -- what did they call? The campaign they had -- co-prosperity sphere, co-prosperity sphere. They were going to create the whole Pacific into what they called -- that was their ambition, to create the co-prosperity sphere among -- in fact, they -- they got every -- everything, Hong Kong, you know, every -- Taiwan, everything, everyplace in the -- in that area.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Was under Japanese control?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh. Except it was good that the -- in the battle of Bataan and Corregidor, they were able to stand it until they could. And here, the Fil-- -- the Filipino and American soldiers fought side by side and they were waiting for the promise that the Armed Forces would come back, U.S. Armed Forces would come back and help them. But no. What happened at the time was they brought all the forces to Europe. And so what happened with -- when Bataan fell, they -- they had gone through the Death March, you know, and they were not fed as war prisoners. And when they went through the Death March, they killed them if they asked for a -- if they were -- if they were passing by streams of water, they would bayonet them or -- they didn't want them to survive.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: What is the Death March? I'm not --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: The Death March. You see the Death March, when the Japanese -- when Bataan fell into the hands of the Japanese forces, they took all the Filipino and American soldiers under their -- under their command and they started walking from Bataan to another town. I don't know how many -- how many -- how many mile -- how many miles it is, and they -- end there. Because Bataan fell in April of 1942, and April is the hottest season in the Philippines. And when you walk under the sun with no water, you would die of dehydration. So the soldiers were -- you know, if they can -- if they can see someplace where there was water, they tried to get that water, but yet at the expense of their life. And some of the Filipino people could not -- although they very much like to give them what they needed at that point, couldn't do anything because -- or else they be killed, they will be the ones killed. And so that when these soldiers came out, when they were freed after that -- that time, they were -- they were imprisoned in what they call Capas, Capas, Tarlac. In fact, today there is a memorial there, and it signified the place where they were imprisoned, both Americans and Filipino forces. And they were crowded, no sanitary conditions. Everything was really to the detriment of the soldiers. And finally they were freed, and so they took -- they took them by -- I think they used a train for bringing them back to Manila. And I know my -- my cousin -- my two cousins came back. They were like living dead, because you couldn't recognize them. They were -- they were so haggard, their -- their arms were as small as this, their legs. Because they -- so that was the thing that happened. They were just like, you know, those pictures that you saw in Europe? You know, that was almost how. We called them the living dead. And in fact, one of my cousins died from those effect of war. But fortunately I did survive.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Do you think -- why do you think? Because you were with the guerillas and you hid in the mountains?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, for one thing, I think part of it was that. But on the other hand, the American forces came at the right time at the right place.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: So part of it was just good fortune on your part.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. But then there was this great loss in the family, so... but anyway, we never -- we never knew where my father was buried or my -- or my uncle. And this is how I sometimes see those families who are victims of September 11, 'cause they don't seem to have a closure to it.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: You know? But I think one of the things that helped us or helped me, especially, was my faith in God, in Jesus Christ. `Cause I had this prayer in one part of my life, and I asked God -- 'cause my father was this. He did not go to church. He was not a churchly person. And if he went to church, it was always during Christmas and Holy Week and Easter Sunday. And so I wasn't so sure that he'd be saved, you know, according to -- according to my faith in Jesus Christ. But I have seen some facets in his life where he believed that the Golden Rule should be the rule of his life, and that was always what he told us. There was a lesson that he taught us, was do unto others as you would have others do unto you. And he always looked at the human perspective, humanity, you know. He was that. And then -- anyway, I was so concerned whether he -- whether he would have that eternal life. And the thing that happened was in 1942, my -- my youngest brother died on December 23rd, two days before Christmas.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Before Christmas.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: And he died of meningitis. And the thing that happened was, when he -- my brother was dying, he said -- I was there. I don't know why I always have been with my father, you know. And so he said to my brother, he said, "Chito" -- that was the nickname of my brother. "Chito," he said, "you are the best Christmas gift I can send to your mother." Because my mother died March 18, 1941, and that was December 1942, you know. He said, "You're the best Christmas gift that I can send to your mother. And when you see them all, your mom -- your momma," he said, "your grand -- your grandpa, everybody" -- he was naming them, and he said, "tell them merry Christmas." And to me as a teenager, it was funny. I said, what in the world is this man saying, you know? I thought it was so funny, you know. But then I -- I think I matured from that, and then I really had this -- after that I said, well, after all, I think my father believe in the eternal life. So I prayed hard and I said to -- I pray. You know, one of my pastimes is praying. I believe in prayer, you know. So I was praying, and I said, Lord, I said, please give me something that I can hold on that my father is in your eternal presence at this moment. And you know what happened? A few nights after that I saw him in a dream. He was in a -- wore his white hat, he wore his white suit, and he was smiling. And I said, thank you, Lord. I know he's in your presence. And that was my closure. And that's why -- the reason my heart fills for those victims of -- you know, those who have been left behind, because they seem to have not -- do not have a closure. You must have to have that or else that will be something that you will carry throughout your life that will be something of a burden or... so I -- I don't know whether -- but this is -- but this is how I feel about it. But...

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Do you have -- did you make very close friends through that period? Are there any of those people that you still know? Have you kept contact with anyone that you met during that time? Was it possible to make and keep friends?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: You mean in the guerillas?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Yes, during that time, you know, fellow soldiers or fellow guerillas?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, I should say that the medical aid man who was with me became a brigadier general, but he died also. And then our -- I think most of them. The lieutenant -- the lieutenant I was with on our trip on that caribou thing, he also died.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: During the war?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No, after the war.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: After the war.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Most of them died after the war. And -- and then also our battalion -- our sub-medical battalion commander also died. So I don't really have any contact with them.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Did you become close with them during that time? Was that difficult?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Oh, yeah, um-hmm. Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Did you keep in touch while they were -- I mean, through the years while they were alive? Were you able to stay in contact?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No, because we went to different -- we all went different places. And I know Pedro -- Pedro Aviles (ph), he went back to high school after that. And then he went -- he went to the Philippine Military Academy, and I never saw him that after. And then later on during the Marcos time, I saw his name in the papers. He was a brigadier general. But later he died.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Actually, at those times in Korea and China, the Japanese gathered the Korean and Chinese women to serve the Japanese soldier for the sexual service. So it's the same in the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, they took some woman.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Teenager or twenties.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. They -- they took some women. They were told -- they were called comfort -- comfort women, to give them their sexual desires.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: So they -- just to bring a car on the street and they gather the womens. So one day they lost their daughter, Sun Ye. So they don't know where they are. So because they made some young daughters to marry some other friends or something to avoid that kind of service.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, in the Philippines we have a few of them who are still living, and they -- and they tried to -- they tried to claim compensation from the Japanese government. But the Japanese government has already said their apology, but the women still want compensation. There's --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Financial compensation?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh, yeah. They called them the comfort women.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: But fortunately I was not one of those. But there were some -- there -- they are much older than I am now. But I think there must be three, four, five alive.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Do you still bear resentment against the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Why do you think -- what got you through that?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: What made you -- was it your faith in --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, it was my faith. There was -- there was a religious -- I had a religious experience. And there was a missionary by the name of _______ Jones --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: There in the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: -- who came to the Philippines. He was an American Methodist missionary to India. And when I was in -- when I was in deaconess school -- see, I went to a school for -- to train myself as a church worker, woman church worker in the Philippine, called deaconesses. And when he went there in 1948, he had a -- he had what they called a peace campaign. And so he spoke to us. He spoke to several churches in Manila. And in one of his services -- you know, we always attended the services every night. And then he said, "I'm going to Japan," he said. "And I know that the Japanese people have done you so much harm and so much -- so many of you have been hurt by what they did. So many lives have been lost because of they did," he said. But he gave us a message on forgiveness and that you must forgive your enemies and forgiving must be -- you must forgive seventy times seventy -- seven times seventy. That is -- that's 490, so it means it's an endless forgiving, you know. So at the last moment, when he asked us if he would be the ambassador of goodwill and peace to the Japanese people, "Will you -- will you please raise your hands and allow me to be your ambassador to the Japanese people and express to them your forgiveness?"

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: At what point was this, what year?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: And so, you know, at that point I was in a dilemma. I said, if I -- I like to be loyal to my father's memory. But on the other hand, I said, Jesus said you must forgive seventy times seven. And I said, well, that was my faith. And so I opted for what Jesus has taught, and so I raised my hands. But my -- my tears were coming down. And then my next experience came again when I came to the United States in 1961. In `62 I was with -- I was with a Japanese Fulbright scholar, a girl, and we became sleepmates in the bus. We were going to attend the Methodist Student Movement Conference in Tillamook, Oregon. And we became sleepmates in the bus. We were always together. And while we were sitting together, I told her about what has happened to my family, what the Japanese people have done. And he said -- she said, "Dorinda, I am very sorry. I was just a little girl," she said, "and I didn't know anything about it." We just -- I said, well, I -- I had this religious experience and I've forgiven the Japanese people. And so more than a year ago I had a Japanese family whom I taught English conversation, the whole family. Now they write to me and they call me their -- they told their -- their daughter, who was three years old when they were here, to call me their American grandma. And that's one of the things that they gave me, that figurine there of a child with a bird. And every -- twice a year I hear from them and they've sent me things. So I really do not have anything against them anymore.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Can you just go back to when the war ended and then what -- what happened, and how you got here to the United States, and kind of just, you know, chronologically --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, the thing that happened was, in 1946 I went back to Manila.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: The war had ended.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh. 1946, and then I start -- I thought that maybe I would go -- I would get into business school.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Were the conditions very hard then?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, it still -- still it was. You still -- it was a time of rebuilding and starting to rebuilding the country. But I -- I went to Manila and I took a course in shorthand. Because during the Japanese time my father never believed in what the Japanese were doing. Although the public schools were open, what the Japanese did was -- you know, when -- when we were under the United States, we studied U.S. history, you know, and history -- U.S. history and government and all that thing. And you know what they did with those history books? They just burned them. And my father said, "Not one of my children will ever go to Japanese schools." So we never went to school during the Japanese time. Although most of the students went back, but we never. So my sister and I took typing lessons instead. And then right after the war was over, I said, well -- in `46, well, I have this typing background, so maybe I can get into shorthand. So I -- but later on I went back to the province, and then I was given a scholarship to finish my high school in a Methodist high school. And then I was also given a scholarship to go to this boarding school, the Harris Memorial School, which trained deaconesses, the women church workers of the Methodist Church. I was given a scholarship there, and at the same time I also was given under the Philippine -- under the Philippine government I was allowed to use my GI bills of rights, my educational benefits. But compared to the rest of the collegiate courses, my -- my field was not as expensive as that because the Methodist Church in the -- in the United States subsidized the school, and so we did not -- we did not pay so much like the rest.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: How was it that your -- your work in the guerillas was recognized by the government and then you given these official papers? How did that come about?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, we were interviewed. We were -- we were interviewed. Two times we were interviewed.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: After the war.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: After the war. We were --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: By your government or the United States?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: United States. In fact, this one -- this one paper here signed by Santa Romana, it says here -- it's not very clear. It says -- the last name is Santa Romana, and he's chairperson of the TDG, which is the Terminal Date Guerilla. And he's -- I don't know how many copies this has been --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Should we stop?

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: No, it's still going on.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Okay. Sorry.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: So anyway, we were interviewed twice, and so that's how they were able to classify us. And -- and then that's how the records stand, you know. And they interviewed us twice. We appeared before, like, -- I think they -- they were with U.S. Army, but they were Filipinos.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Then you were given formal recognition for your work and efforts in the war --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- at that point?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: At that point, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: And then from that you were able to get assistance, you were qualified for assistance in schooling and things?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Oh, no?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: When you later went to school, that wasn't sponsored by the government?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: That was not sponsored by the U.S. government.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: It was sponsored by the Philippine government.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: So we -- and then I came -- I went back to school. After I finished serving the Methodist Church in the Philippines, I went back to school to take -- to take my undergraduate degree, my bachelor of arts degree in English and --

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: In English.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: And then I -- I applied in one of the seminaries in United States. And I was accepted in Iowa School of Theology. In fact, a number of people I have met along the way, they will tell me that they were in the war during the Philippines, you know, like the vice-president of the seminary. And when I came to him and he said -- you see, I came to the United States, I was itinerated as a speaker to speak on the missions in the Philippines for three weeks in Michigan. And I earned my first 400 dollars in the United States by speaking for missions. And so when he approached me and he said, "Dorinda," he said, "do you have money?" I was surprised. Well, he was -- he was the vice-president of the student affairs and he looked into the situation of incoming students coming from the Philippines. Maybe he knew -- he knew I didn't have that much money. And I said, well -- I said to him, well, I said, sir, I have -- I said, I earned my first 400 dollars. So the school gave me scholarship and room rent and everything, except that I served in the church in Nebraska, commuting every weekend, 900 miles every weekend on the train.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: In Nebraska?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. From Denver I commuted by train. I used to be on the CBNQ, if you are familiar with the CBNQ.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Every weekend?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Every weekend.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Nine hundred miles?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Uh-huh. Four hundred miles -- 450 miles one way, 450 miles another way. I would leave -- I would leave Denver on Friday night and then come back to Denver early Monday morning in time -- we didn't have class on Mondays. So we started classes on Tuesdays, then went back again on Friday. But I did that for my first year. My second year I was hired in a Denver church to do educational assistance work.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: So this is in the early sixties?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: So you would have been late twenties?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: No. I was 34 when I came over.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Thirty-four. Okay.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: So I was 34 when I came.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: What was your motivation at that time? Were you thinking about careers or? What were you thinking?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, I was very good in Spanish when I was in college because in the Philippines, for four years you have to have 24 hours of Spanish. You cannot graduate from college unless you have that, and this is what we call the Philippine Spanish Law, and all college students were required to do that. And I was very good in that because maybe -- my father was Spanish speaking. And although we were not Spanish speaking at home, we understood some of the things that he would say in Spanish and all that. But -- and I had an interest in the language, and so I became one of the best students, and thinking that eventually I'll go to University -- apply for a scholarship to the University of Madrid for my master's degree. And on the other hand, because I had this religious background, religious work background, I decided to apply in the United States. I said, whichever comes first, that's where I'm going. Well, the seminaries in the United States started answering my letters of application, so I came to the United States. And also, I had another -- I have a person who backed me up, one of the -- shall I say, one of the greatest laymen of the Methodist Church in the United States. And he came to know me, I came to know him. And he was one of the -- you know, Billy Graham said that he was -- he was one of the greatest evangelists that Billy Graham knew. And so with his letters to the seminary, he backed me up, so I was able to get there. But the rest of the seminaries that answered my letter, usually they ask me, well, you have to get a letter from your bishop. Well, our bishop, I know him very well, but my bishop didn't like families to be separated. At that time I was married, and I knew that if I got the letter from him, he'll never permit me to leave the Philippines. So I didn't ask him for a reference. But the other seminaries, two seminaries, did ask for bishop's letters. So I said, I'm not going to ask the bishop, so I went on my own. And my husband and I were married eleven -- nine years when I came to the States. And so when people started asking me, well, "Oh," they said, "your -- your husband is there and you are here?" Yeah, I said. "How is that," most Americans, you know? Well, it's just like in the Army, the men leaves the wife, so now it's me leaving my husband.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Did he eventually come?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yes, eventually he came. And then he -- he worked at Purdue for 28 years, and he died seven years ago.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: How did you get here?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Here?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Oh, well, anyway, that's very interesting.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: You have to catch us up here.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah, because the thing was, after seminary graduation in 1963, I started -- well, I had some -- I couldn't work because I was on a student visa. You know, at that time I couldn't work. I was on a student visa. But after -- after graduation I had a big, major surgery. I had a major surgery and I -- my husband came for my graduation, but he couldn't work because he was on a tourist visa. So -- but the churches that I worked with supported me. And then Immigration -- oh, no. I asked for permission to work from Immigration, and Immigration referred my letter to the school. And the school reg- -- seminary registrar said, as far as we know, Dorinda Guillermo graduated in June 1963, but she underwent this major surgery and she needs to work to gain -- to earn. So they -- so at that time -- I started also -- before that letter came, you know, I started working with school lunch program district in Denver, one of the chair -- one of the school districts there, because the women of the church were -- the women of the church in that -- women's group in the church, they had the manager cook of the school district program. And so they said, "Dorinda, we need another person in our -- in our food service. Would you like to be the salad girl?" Sure, I said. I like to learn. And at that time the wages was a dollar fifty, free lunch. That was all that -- and so then that was the time when I asked for permission to work. So they decided to write -- write the school registrar, and then they called me for an interview. And then the Immigration officer -- you know, most Immigration officers, they tried to -- when they interrogate you, they are -- I liken them to be like... what this is? Unkind and all those, you know, that they don't see you as a human being or something like that, you know. So anyway, he called -- I was called for an interview, and -- and then he asks me, "Did you graduate already?" he asked me. Yes, sir. And he said, "I understand you're working. Where are you working now?" I said, oh, I work in the school lunch program, District Number 5. "What do you do there?" Salad girl. "How much do you earn?" A dollar fifty an hour. "How many hours do you work?" Five hours. "You, with a master's degree, working in a kitchen? Where will I get my food? How will I live?" And so he -- then at that time he became a little bit kinder and he said, "now," he said, "what I want you to do is find a church that will employ you where you can do practical training for your major field of study. You can earn some money and save your money and go back to the Philippines." That is what he said to me. And so I started looking for a -- for a church after I worked in the school lunch program. And I was able to find work in First Methodist Church in Des Plains, Illinois, which is a suburb of Chicago. And at that time, when I moved from Denver to Chicago, the church asked me, how much furniture did I have? I said, if you consider a card table and a -- and an ironing board as furniture, that's all. Anyway, they were so kind. They found an apartment for me and then they furnished the apartment and all that thing. But I was the victim of racism there the two years I was there, and so I had to find another job, you know. But that -- at that time racism wasn't as much issue in -- in Denver, you know.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: As it was in the Chicago area?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: As it was in the Chicago area. But the thing that happened in the Chicago area was they started -- well, you know, as a director of Christian education, they told me to do something with the Christmas program and said I have to work with a young adults, you know. Sure, I said, I like to do that. And so we -- I planned the Christmas program and bringing in young adults, elementary school teachers, bankers, you know, stock brokers, coming in to work with us in that school program, in that school Christmas program, only to find out that I was stepping on somebody's toes, an older woman who used to do this job year in and year out. And then she talked to the pastor and all these things, and there I was blacklisted and everything. And so pastor said to me, "Well," he said, "it's time for you to go." There was no question at all, no nothing at all. I only came to know about what happened, it was because of the members. Because I didn't have anyplace to go and because they also had signed the affidavit of support, in any way if I ever go out -- if I get financially unable, they will be the one to take care of me. So the church people were -- were for me. And so anyway, I said, it's okay, but I'll -- I'll work. I said, I'll -- I have to find another job. So I came -- I came to Lafayette and I worked at First -- no, Congress Church across Columbia Park. And then after four years I worked at First Church, and I was there for six years. So -- but that is how I -- but I had been a victim of racism even in North Angela (ph) Conference 'cause, you see, I went back for my second degree, for my master's degree in divinity, thinking, hoping to be a pastor. And I went back to -- I went back to seminary for my master of divinity, and it took me two years to finish it instead of three because I had previous units from the former seminary. So Garrett Evangelical Theological Seminary allowed me 20 units to work towards my master of divinity. So I -- I went to school after 17 years of not being in school. So I became -- even my ordination was -- were all in -- had some issues, you know. And you think that racism is not present in Indiana, but at that point -- I think in the church at that point I felt that it was ________, especially among the -- but the only thing -- the only thing that I have felt was that I am -- I said, I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, I said, and nothing can separate me from him, even the higher-ups in the Methodist Church, I said. And the thing is -- the thing that really bothered me was that they started saying that north Indiana churches do not like women of clergy, clergy of color, and over 55. And I was over 55, so I had three strikes against me. And the only thing that I could do at that point was when they had those words out, I wrote a letter in our United Methodist paper and I said, different is beautiful. And I said, if God created all people white, this would be a boring place to live in. But God in his greatness created everything different -- every person different from one another. He created things differently so that this world would be more beautiful. That's -- that was the only reply I said. And so anyway, that's one reason I never reached my -- and then besides, I do not drive. They always had that, and I talked to the bishop. I said, when God called me into the ministry, he didn't ask me if I could drive, I said. And yet we preach in the church that we -- God accepts us as we are. We should accept people as they are, but we never do that. That's what I told our bishop. That's one reason why maybe they do not like me, because I talk back.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: You're outspoken.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Yeah. But I like to say something, you know. Just like what happened in memorial service, a Memorial Day program. It said in the paper, on the program, it says there, remembering veterans, it said. We do not -- we do not forget, it said, and said something like, celebrating the 60th anniversary of the fall of Bataan. I went there, my first time to go to a Memorial Day program, and they told me that the essence of the program was to honor or to memorialize the veterans of World War -- fall of Bataan. Never a thing was said during all those speeches about Bataan, and then they offered floral offerings. Not even maybe one rose was offered for Bataan veterans. And I said, if you honor a person, if you memorialize a person, you say something about that person. But never a word. And so Paulson (ph) said to me, "You write the Memorial Day committee." I haven't done it yet. I told them it's -- I said, it's water under the bridge. "Oh, Dorinda, you have to correct it." So I said, well, if I have the time and inspiration to write, I'm going to write it, I said. So that's -- and I -- and I wrote _______ April 9th about the fall of Bataan and the equitable...

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: If there's one thing that you could say -- because we don't have much time. We're only allowed to do 90 minutes.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: -- your experience from the war, what could you tell humanity, do you think?

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Humanity? Especially I would like to say that there is no win/win in the war. Everything is a loss. And I would say that if I -- if it would ever be possible, not to have war again. And the thing that I could say is, if we could just get into the situation of really respecting one another, respect each other's values, because each one of us has values that could really make the place -- the world a better place to live in. And I -- and I'm not so sure that peace could be attained by too much war. And I have gone through that and I am -- I'm not going to go through again, you know, another one again. Of course, I'm 75 years old, so maybe they will not call me anymore. I'll not be involved in it. But I really feel that it is really no win/win, is how I feel about it. I don't know how you feel about it. Like this -- like this war in Afghanistan, you know, I'm not so sure. Those tribal lords -- war lords over there, how can you control them? They'll go back to their old ways. I don't -- I'm not so sure what's going on. I -- I read the papers, and Palestine -- and Palestine and Israel situation. I -- I read the Pakistani and India conflict and tribal wars in Africa, and even in the Philippines right now. I just can't imagine what will happen if the Third World War would ever come. It could be the annihilation of the human race it if it ever be. So if we don't feel -- if we are not going to do anything about it then I think, you know... but on the other hand, God created this world in love, and he loved the world so much that he brought his -- gave his only begotten son, that whosoever believes in him, will not -- will not perish, but will have eternal life. And so if we don't have that peace in this life, maybe we could have it in the next life. And who knows? Maybe we'll see each other there.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: I hope so. You are an extraordinary human being.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, I hope so. I'm just trying to do what God wants me to do. I'm also -- I'm also just as human as anybody, and I have my flaws and my mistakes and my failures and -- but a lot I think has happened to my life, that I always thank God for everything that has happened in my life. And then as I look ahead I said, God, dear God, I said, you have seen me through the years of my life, 75 years, so what do I have in the years ahead? So I trust that the best is yet to come. Because, what you will do?

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Is there anything you'd like to say before we --

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: I think I have said it all.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: You have been wonderful. Thank you so much.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: You're very welcome. I have never really had this kind of interview. This is my first interview, something like this, on the war.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: Someone should write your story in a book.

sp.speaker: Sung Hee Park
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Well, the thing is, my father told me a lot of stories while we were together during the Japanese occupation, and if the Lord will still give me some years ahead, my plan after moving to Texas is to write our family story, because I seem to have the most of it. And I want -- I belong to the fourth generation of our family, and I want the younger generation to know more about it. And if I don't do it, nobody will know where they came from. Even my older sister, she is amazed at how much I know. I said, because you didn't ask questions and you didn't stay with dad. I said, we had our time together. In fact, I felt lost more with my father's death than with my mom's because of the years we had together.

sp.speaker: Bob Thrash
sp.p: And got so close.

sp.speaker: Dorinda Guillermo
sp.p: Conclusion of interview]
